headline: A record heat wave hits the United States

sources.title: US heat wave death toll grows
19 deaths in New Jersey likely connected to heat wave, officials say
Heat-related deaths mount after historic Fourth of July heat wave broiled eastern US
July 4 Heat Wave Shatters More Than 148 Records Across The Eastern US (video, FOX Weather)

chunks.text: A dangerous [[heat wave]] {{heated up}} much of the United States over the July 4 holiday weekend. A large [[heat dome]] [[settled]] over the country, and the [[extreme]] heat {{set in}} from the Midwest to the East Coast. Officials said about 40 million people were under a heat [[alert]] on Sunday. Weather [[forecasters]] [[warned of]] a serious danger to people's health.

verbs.wrong: To stay hot for many days
verbs.why: An engine heats up after a long drive, and an oven heats up before you can bake anything. A dangerous heat wave heated up much of the country over the Fourth of July weekend.

verbs.wrong: To announce a new weather warning system
verbs.correct: To begin and seem likely to continue
verbs.why: Boredom sets in after hours of waiting, and panic sets in the moment the elevator stops. Extreme heat set in across the country from the Midwest all the way to the East Coast.

chunks.text: Forecasters said the heat wave [[broke many old records]]. Temperatures {{shot up}} above 100 degrees Fahrenheit in many cities. In Washington, D.C., the temperature reached 103 degrees on July 4, which officials said was a new record. High [[humidity]] made the air feel even hotter. Overnight, the air did not {{cool down}} much, and [[the low]] stayed near 80 degrees, so many people could not {{cool off}}.

verbs.wrong: To stay at a very high level
verbs.why: Ticket prices shoot up right before a concert sells out, and a fever can shoot up overnight. Temperatures shot up above 100 degrees in many cities, reaching 103 in Washington, D.C., on July 4.
A hot pizza cools down before you eat it, and a room usually cools down once the sun sets. Overnight the air barely cooled down at all, and the low stayed near 80 degrees.

verbs.wrong: To take a rest in the shade
verbs.why: People drink cold water to cool off after a hike, or sit in the shade to cool off after a run. With the overnight low stuck near 80 degrees, many people could not cool off at all.

chunks.text: Officials said the heat wave was [[blamed for]] [[at least]] 24 deaths [[across the country]] during the week. In New Jersey, state health officials said about 22 deaths were [[linked to]] the heat. Officials also {{pointed out}} that extreme heat is one of the [[deadliest]] kinds of weather in the United States. Officials asked people to {{look out for}} older neighbors and anyone living without [[air conditioning]].

verbs.correct: To tell someone a fact they may not know
verbs.why: A friend might point out a spelling error, and a coach might point out a mistake in your form. Officials pointed out that extreme heat is one of the deadliest kinds of weather in the country.

verbs.correct: To take care to protect someone
verbs.why: Neighbors look out for each other during a storm, and lifeguards look out for swimmers who drift too far. During the heat wave, officials asked people to look out for older neighbors and anyone without air conditioning.

chunks.text: To help people {{deal with}} the heat, many cities opened a [[cooling center]] where [[residents]] could stay cool. Officials asked people to {{carry on}} drinking water and to rest indoors during the hottest hours. Some [[outdoor]] events were {{called off}} [[for safety]]. By early the next week, forecasters said the heat would finally {{let up}} as cooler air [[moved in]].

verbs.wrong: To collect data about heat-related deaths
verbs.correct: To take action to solve a problem
verbs.why: A city might deal with heavy traffic by adding more buses, and a school might deal with crowded halls by hiring extra staff. Many cities opened cooling centers to help residents deal with the dangerous heat.

verbs.wrong: To remember to do something important
verbs.why: A band might carry on playing even after the rain starts, and an old tradition can carry on for generations. During the heat wave, officials asked people to carry on drinking water through the hottest hours of the day.

verbs.wrong: To move an event indoors for safety
verbs.why: An airline calls off a flight because of fog, and a school calls off recess when a thunderstorm gets close. During the worst of the heat wave, some outdoor events were called off for everyone's safety.

A bad headache can let up once you drink some water, and heavy traffic often lets up after a game ends. Forecasters said the dangerous heat would finally let up early the next week as cooler air arrived.

ex: The engine started to heat up after the long drive.
The whole region will heat up again later this week.
The oven needs a few minutes to heat up before baking.

wordDefs.def: Happening or used outside

wordDefs.def: Trapped hot air that sits over a region
ex: A heat dome covered the whole Midwest.

wordDefs.def: People who say what the weather will do

ex: The alert covered fifteen states.

wordDefs.def: Did better than any earlier result
ex: The runner broke many old records at the state meet.

ex: The low tonight will be near freezing.

wordDefs.def: Arrived and began to affect an area

mainIdea.s: A heat wave heated up much of the country and broke many records over the July 4 weekend. Officials blamed the heat for at least two dozen deaths nationwide.
mainIdea.why: The article says at least two dozen deaths nationwide were blamed on the heat wave, which broke many records.

mainIdea.s: Extreme heat spread across the nation last week, and officials say it has killed more than a hundred people. Cities opened cooling centers to help residents.
mainIdea.why: Close, but this overstates the deaths. The article says at least two dozen people died, not more than a hundred.

mainIdea.s: Dry weather and wind pushed wildfires across the western United States last month. Firefighters said the fires damaged many houses before crews stopped them.
mainIdea.why: This describes wildfires in the western United States, a separate event. The article covers heat wave deaths, not wildfires.

tf.s: Overnight, the air did not cool down much, and the low stayed near 80 degrees.
tf.why: Correct. The air did not cool down, which means it did not become cooler; the low stayed near 80 degrees.

tf.s: The extreme heat cooled off from the Midwest to the East Coast.
tf.why: The correct verb is set in. The heat began and continued across the region; it did not cool off, which would mean become less hot.

tf.s: Temperatures let up above 100 degrees Fahrenheit in many cities.
tf.why: The correct verb is shot up. Temperatures rose quickly above 100 degrees; let up would mean they became less strong.

tf.s: Over the holiday weekend, a heat wave heated up much of the United States.
tf.why: Correct. The heat wave heated up (made much hotter) large parts of the country. Heat up means to become or make something hotter.

tf.s: Some outdoor events were called off for safety.
tf.why: Correct. The events were called off, which means they were canceled for safety.

tf.s: Officials asked people to call off drinking water during the heat.
tf.why: The correct verb is carry on. Officials asked people to continue drinking water; call off would mean to cancel it.
